intro: LLMs don't read English — they read numbers. This episode reveals the secret language of tokens, token IDs, and tokenizers. Understanding tokenization helps you write better prompts, manage costs, and avoid common misconceptions.

sections.heading: Tokens & Token IDs
sections.definition: When you type 'These notes are awesome', the LLM doesn't see words — it sees numbers. Text is broken into tokens, and each token gets a token ID. The model predicts the next token ID, which maps back to text.
points: Sentence → broken into tokens → converted to token IDs → fed to LLM
LLM predicts next token ID, not next word directly
Tokenizer does the breaking — different models use different tokenizers
One word ≠ one token always — 'awesome' might become 'awe' + 'some'

sections.heading: Subword tokenization & BPE
sections.definition: Subword tokenization splits words into reusable pieces. Byte Pair Encoding (BPE) merges common character pairs into tokens — so 'un', 'trust', 'able' can combine into 'untrustable' as 3 tokens.
points: Common pieces become single tokens — reused across many words
BPE used by OpenAI; SentencePiece-BPE used by Meta Llama
Tokenizer vocabulary = fixed list of all tokens the model recognizes
Tokenization depends on vocabulary, not grammar or word meaning
'undone' can be 1 token if it's common in vocabulary — not always split

sections.heading: English vs other languages
sections.definition: Same meaning in different languages produces different token IDs. English is more token-efficient; Hinglish and Hindi often use more tokens for the same content — which means higher cost.
points: No meaning in token IDs — just mapping based on text patterns
'I am learning AI' vs 'Mai AI seekh raha hu' — different token counts
Modern tokenizers handle Hinglish well despite spelling variations
English takes fewer tokens → cheaper and faster for same content
Vocabulary size affects how efficiently a model handles each language

sections.heading: Special characters, emojis & code
sections.definition: Emojis, code, spaces, and capitalization all affect tokenization. Adding or removing a space can change the token count. Everything is mapped in the vocabulary.
points: Emojis and special characters have their own token mappings
Spaces, dashes, curly braces — all change how text is tokenized
Tokenization fertility = average tokens per word (lower = cheaper/faster)
Try OpenAI tokenizer or tiktokenizer.vercel.app to see live tokenization

sections.heading: Context window
sections.definition: The context window is the model's short-term working memory — the max amount of tokenized text it can process at once. It includes system instructions, your messages, documents, and tool outputs.
points: Context window = max tokens model can 'see' in one request
Includes everything: system prompt, chat history, files, tool results
Shared between your input and the model's generated output
Overflow? Truncate input, summarize old messages, split into separate chats
Longer prompt ≠ better result — tokens directly affect API cost

sections.heading: Common misconceptions
sections.definition: Many students get tokenization wrong. Clearing these up saves you from bad assumptions about how LLMs work.
points: ❌ One token = one word → ✅ Words can split into multiple tokens
❌ All models use same tokenizer → ✅ Each model has its own
❌ Token ID represents meaning → ✅ IDs are just lookup numbers
❌ One emoji = one token → ✅ Can be multiple tokens
❌ Larger context = perfect memory → ✅ Context has limits and costs
❌ More tokens = better answers → ✅ Quality depends on prompt, not length
